title: Linen, waste and spill escalation
audience: Cleaners and cleaning supervisors who handle linen, general waste, and spills in residential aged care, clinics, dental practices and NDIS settings in any Australian state or territory.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NHMRC, Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) (no page date shown; document dated 2019), only partly confirmed; NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 (November 2021), Core Module (no page date shown), only partly confirmed; Safe Work Australia, Duties of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) (no date shown).
learningOutcomes: Distinguish ordinary linen and general waste from items that the facility treats as potentially infectious, and state the handling rule for each.
Recognise a body-fluid spill, a sharp or an uncertain waste item, and state that these are escalated to trained personnel under the facility procedure.
Describe the immediate containment steps for a spill a cleaner is authorised to attend, and the stop-and-escalate steps for one they are not.
Record the item, location, action and escalation for linen, waste and spill events.

instruction.heading: Linen and general waste: the ordinary rules
instruction.body: Ordinary linen and general waste are handled under the facility's linen and waste procedure. Bag and close linen at the point of collection, do not shake it, and keep it away from your face and clean stock. Place general waste in the correct bin, and do not overfill it. The facility decides which items go in which stream, and it may treat some linen as potentially infectious, for example after a known exposure. Follow the colour, label and stream the facility uses, and do not mix streams. If you are unsure which stream an item belongs in, do not guess. Set it aside and ask.

instruction.heading: Potentially infectious items and uncertain waste
instruction.body: Some items are treated by the facility as potentially infectious, and a cleaner may not be trained to decide that from appearance. These can include linen or dressings soaked with body fluid, items from an isolation area, and any waste whose origin you do not know. Do not open, sort, compact or reach into a bag or bin to identify its contents. Close it if it is safe to do so, label it as the facility directs, place it in the designated holding area, and tell the supervisor. The facility decides the stream, and the handling is done by staff trained for it.

instruction.heading: Body-fluid spills: what a cleaner may and may not do
instruction.body: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare recommend that anyone cleaning a spill wears gloves and other personal protective equipment appropriate to the task. Where the facility has trained you and written your role into the spill procedure, you may contain and clean a small, identified, non-blood spill using the approved product. For blood or other body-fluid spills, larger spills, spills of unknown origin, spills that have reached carpet or soft furnishings, or spills near sharps, do not clean them unless the facility has trained and authorised you in writing. Restrict access, keep people away, and call the trained spill response person. Do not wipe a spill to reduce the visible mess before the trained person arrives.

instruction.heading: Sharps and clinical waste: escalate, do not handle
instruction.body: Sharps, such as needles, lancets and broken glass that may be contaminated, are not handled by a cleaner by hand. Do not pick them up, reach into a sharps container, push sharps into a bin, or attempt to recap a needle. If you find a sharp, stop, keep others away, and call the designated sharps response person under the facility procedure. If you are stuck or cut, follow the exposure procedure at once. Clinical waste is handled by staff trained and authorised for it, and the cleaner's role is to recognise it, keep it separate, and escalate.

instruction.heading: Worked case: the unidentified spill by the laundry trolley
instruction.body: You find a wet, unidentified mark near a laundry trolley in a corridor. It may be a spill of body fluid, or it may be water. Do not touch it or clean it. Put a warning sign or cone in place if the facility provides one, keep people away, and call the trained spill response person and your supervisor. Record the location, the time, the description and who you called. Only after the trained person has assessed the spill and given a written instruction should a cleaner clean it, and only using the procedure the instruction gives.

procedure: Identify the item: ordinary linen, general waste, a potentially infectious item, a sharp, or a spill.
For ordinary linen and general waste, bag and close it at the collection point and place it in the correct stream without shaking or sorting.
For a potentially infectious or uncertain item, close it if safe, label it as directed, and place it in the designated holding area. Do not open or sort it.
For a sharp, stop, keep others away, call the sharps response person, and follow the exposure procedure if injured.
For a spill, restrict access, put up a warning if provided, and call the trained spill response person and your supervisor.
Clean a spill only if you are trained and authorised in writing for that spill type, and wear the gloves and protection the facility specifies.
Record the item or spill, location, time, action taken and the person called.

workedExamples.situation: You find a plastic bag of linen by a bathroom door. The bag is damp at the base and you cannot tell whether the dampness is water or body fluid.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you handle the bag?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not open the bag or sort the linen. Close the bag if it is safe, label it as the facility directs, place it in the designated holding area, and tell the supervisor. The facility decides the stream. Record the location, the time and the person told.

workedExamples.situation: A colleague asks you to wipe up a small spill of an unknown liquid on the floor of a resident's room, saying it will take only a moment.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not wipe the spill unless the facility has trained and authorised you for that spill type. The liquid is unknown, so the trained spill response person must assess it. Restrict access, put up a warning if provided, and call the trained person and your supervisor. Record the event.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves and protection for the task, as specified by the facility: {{business:safety.required_ppe}}
Spill kit and warning signage, where provided and where you are trained to use it
Designated holding area and labelled containers for linen and waste streams

commonErrors.error: Sorting through a bag of linen or waste to find out what is in it.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not open or sort potentially infectious or uncertain items. Close, label and escalate.

commonErrors.error: Wiping up a body-fluid spill to tidy the area before the trained person arrives.
commonErrors.prevention: Restrict access and call the trained person. Clean only when trained and authorised for that spill.

commonErrors.error: Picking up a sharp by hand or pushing it into a bin.
commonErrors.prevention: Never handle sharps by hand. Keep others away and call the sharps response person.

commonErrors.error: Putting an uncertain item in the general waste stream to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Set it aside, label it, and ask for the stream to be decided by the trained person.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) recommend that anyone cleaning a spill wears gloves and other personal protective equipment appropriate to the task (Recommendation 12). The guidelines do not, in the text checked, assign spill response to cleaning staff as a group, so the facility's spill procedure defines the role.

The NDIS Practice Standards, Version 4 of November 2021, Core Module, require policies for storing, handling and disposing of infectious waste, including used PPE, that incidents involving infectious material are reported, recorded, investigated and reviewed, and that workers who handle waste are trained.

Licence notice: Handling, collecting or transporting regulated medical or clinical waste off site may require a state or territory permit or licence. This lesson does not grant any waste handling, transport or treatment authority.

Exposure to a sharp or a body fluid is a work health and safety matter. The facility's exposure procedure governs the response, and the Safe Work Australia summary of PCBU duties (page with no date shown) applies to the facility; state adoption should be confirmed for each state and territory.

qualityStandard: The learner sorts five supplied items into the correct stream or into the escalate group, with one reason for each.
The learner names the escalation step for a supplied body-fluid spill, a sharp, and an uncertain bag, without handling the item.
The learner describes the protection and containment steps for an authorised small spill in the facility's procedure, and states when the spill is outside their authority.
The learner records a linen, waste or spill event with location, time, action and person called.
documentationEvidence: Item type, location, time, and the action taken
Spill or sharp escalation: the person called, the time, and the trained person's instruction
Any exposure event, with the first aid and the follow-up notified under the facility procedure
summary: Ordinary linen and general waste follow the facility streams. Do not sort or guess.
Potentially infectious, uncertain and sharp items are not opened or handled by hand. Close, label and escalate.
A body-fluid spill, a large or unknown spill, or any spill near sharps is escalated to trained personnel. Clean only when authorised in writing.
Record every linen, waste and spill event, with the person called and the time.

knowledgeChecks.question: A bag of linen is damp and you cannot tell whether the moisture is water or body fluid. What should you do?
options: Open the bag to check, then put the linen in the right stream once you know what it is and how wet it is
Do not open or sort it. Close and label it as directed, place it in the holding area, and tell the supervisor.
Put it in the general linen bag and forget about it, since the bag will be washed with the rest anyway today

knowledgeChecks.question: You find a body-fluid spill on a corridor floor. What is the correct response?
options: Wipe it up quickly so the corridor is clear for the next person walking through
Cover it with a towel and leave it until the end of the shift, when it can be dealt with
Restrict access and call the trained spill response person and your supervisor.

knowledgeChecks.question: You find a loose needle on the floor of a treatment room. What should you do?
options: Do not handle it by hand. Keep others away and call the designated sharps response person.
Pick it up with a tissue and place it in the general bin, since the tissue protects you
Push it under the bed out of sight until a nurse is free, so it does not get kicked
